readerTitle: What one type of plane tells you about Southwest's strategy
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Southwest, Continental) + 가상 적용 (커피 키오스크)
insight: 전략은 좋은 선택 하나가 아니라 서로를 지탱하는 선택들의 묶음이다.
misconception: 경쟁사의 좋은 기능을 하나씩 따라 하면 따라잡을 수 있다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1996). What Is Strategy? Harvard Business Review.
Southwest Airlines press releases on checked-bag fees (2025) and assigned seating (2026)

factChecks.note: "47년 연속 흑자"는 1973~2019년 기준이며 2020년 팬데믹으로 끊겼습니다. 문구에 "for 47 years in a row"로만 쓰고 이후 상황은 7번 카드에서 다룹니다.
10분 턴어라운드 일화(1972년 항공기 매각)는 Southwest의 공식 역사 자료에 나오는 내용입니다. 정확한 분 단위는 자료마다 조금씩 다릅니다. 카드에는 "about 10 minutes"로 적었습니다.
수하물 유료화(2025년 5월)와 지정 좌석제(2026년 1월)는 게시 직전에 Southwest 보도자료로 다시 확인하세요. 바뀐 시스템의 성과는 아직 평가하기 이릅니다. 카드에도 "open question"으로 적었습니다.
Continental Lite 사례는 Porter(1996)에 나옵니다. 운영 기간은 1993~1995년경입니다.

cards.title: What one type of plane tells you about Southwest's strategy
body: For most of its history, Southwest Airlines flew only one type of aircraft: the Boeing 737.
It sounds like a fleet detail. It was a key part of a business that made a profit for 47 years in a row.

image.label: One choice is a tactic. Strategy is a bundle of choices.
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 기종 비행기 다섯 대가 일렬로 서 있고, 한 대만 빠르게 출발하는 모션 라인. 실제 항공사 로고와 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your customers want assigned seats.
body: You run a low-fare regional airline. Your rival offers assigned seats, free meals and connections through a big hub airport. A survey says your customers would like assigned seats too.

options.text: Add assigned seats and meals to match the rival
options.feedback: Each feature looks small. Together they slow boarding and cleaning, and your low fares depend on turning planes around fast. You'd end up with the rival's costs and your own fares.

options.text: Keep your model and explain what customers get for it
options.feedback: If every part of your model supports low fares, removing one part weakens the others. That's the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Copy only the cheapest feature: free snacks
options.feedback: Cheap on paper. But the question isn't what one feature costs. It's whether it fits the rest of the system.

cards.title: A 10-minute turnaround, born in a crisis.
body: In 1972, Southwest had to sell one of its four planes. To keep its schedule with three, its crews learned to unload, clean and reload a plane in about 10 minutes.
Fast turnarounds meant more flights per plane each day. More flights per plane meant a lower cost per seat. Lower costs meant lower fares.
Much of what Southwest did next was built to protect that speed.

cards.title: Fit between activities
body: **Fit** means a company's activities support each other, so the whole system works better than any single part.
Michael Porter used Southwest as his main example in a 1996 essay, "What Is Strategy?". His point: a strategy isn't one clever choice. It's many choices that reinforce each other.

image.label: Activity map: choices linked by arrows
image.brief: 활동 지도 인포그래픽. 가운데 "Low fares", 주변에 "One plane type", "No assigned seats", "No meals", "Point-to-point routes", "Fast turnarounds"가 화살표로 서로 연결됨.

cards.title: How the pieces lock together.
list: **One plane type:** simpler training, maintenance and spare parts
**Direct routes, smaller airports:** fewer delays, quicker turns
**Quicker turns:** more flights per plane, so **lower fares**
cards.callout: Take out one piece and the others get weaker.
cards.softwareNote: Fit shows up when pricing, product and sales match. A self-serve product with a free trial, low prices and no sales team works because each choice supports the others. Bolt an enterprise sales team onto it, and costs can rise faster than prices.

cards.title: Continental copied the parts, not the system.
body: In 1993, Continental Airlines launched Continental Lite: low fares, no meals, quick turnarounds.
But it ran inside a full-service airline with hub airports, assigned seats, first class and frequent-flyer perks. The pieces worked against each other. Delays at busy hubs broke the quick turns.
Continental Lite lost money and was shut down within about two years.

cards.title: Fit can also make change hard.
body: A tightly connected system is hard for rivals to copy. It's also hard to adjust when customers or costs change.

Under pressure from investors, Southwest began charging for checked bags in 2025 and moved to assigned seating in 2026. Whether its new set of choices fits together as well as the old one is still an open question.

cards.title: Now it's a coffee kiosk.
body: Your kiosk in a train station serves commuters who have about two minutes. Which set of choices fits together best?

options.text: Short menu, order-ahead app, card-only payment
options.feedback: Each choice speeds up the others. A short menu makes drinks fast, pre-orders smooth out the rush, and card-only skips counting change.

options.text: Big menu, comfy seats, table service
options.feedback: A lovely café for the wrong customer. Every choice slows the line for people racing to a train.

options.text: Short menu, plus sandwiches made to order
options.feedback: The sandwiches may sell, but they break the speed the rest of the kiosk is built around. Could they be made ahead instead?

cards.title: Strategy is a set of choices that protect each other.
body: Before adding a feature, ask what it does to the rest of the system.
**Try it today:** list your five most important activities. Draw an arrow wherever one makes another easier. Where are there no arrows?
